sections.report:
I walked the whole-piece section and every line came out yes, so there were no "no" lines to look up in the reference entries. The form has one serious problem: there is no button to submit it. That belongs to the interface section, not this one. I've recorded it under "Couldn't judge from a still" so you can decide where it goes.

**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **Clear purpose:** The heading "Book a workshop seat" (about x 96–397, y 60–95) says what the page is for in one plain verb phrase, naming the action and the thing booked. A first-time viewer can tell what it does at once, so the "can a viewer say in one sentence what this is for" line passes.
- **One consistent style:** The page uses one type family in two weights (bold heading and bold labels), one dark ink colour, and four fields that look the same: same width (about x 96–576), height, grey border, corner radius, and spacing between them. Nothing is ornament. Nothing looks borrowed from another style. The same kind of element looks the same everywhere it appears.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- **No way to send the form (affects the whole piece; filed under interface):** Below the last field (y ≈ 514) the canvas is empty down to y = 800, with no button and no other way to submit. If that's how it's built, people can fill in the form and still can't book. That would be the biggest defect on the page. A still image can't show whether the button failed to load or the screenshot stopped short. Check in a live browser whether a submit button renders below "Notes for the host". If none does, add one that names the action, such as "Book my seat".
- **Inputs give no hint of what they take (interface/text sections):** Every field is a blank single-line box. "Workshop name" looks like free typing rather than a choice from a list. "Preferred date" has no date picker icon and no format hint. "Number of seats" doesn't look like a number field. "Notes for the host" is one line high, so it reads as a short answer rather than room to write. I can't tell from a still whether these become pickers when clicked.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye lands on "Book a workshop seat" at top left (about x 96–397, y 60–95). It then runs down four labelled fields that look exactly alike. The form ends at y ≈ 513 with no submit button, and the right half and bottom third of the canvas are empty. It reads as a plain, generic booking form for someone reserving workshop seats. The image is about one screen (1280×800), so I worked from the whole image.

What matters first:
- One element dominates: **yes**. The title is roughly 28 px bold against roughly 16 px labels, and nothing else competes with it.
- Levels tell apart at a glance: **yes**. There are two text levels (title and labels) with a big step between them and no near-duplicate sizes.
- Headings differ by more than size: **no**. The title and the labels are both bold and both the same near-black, so size is the only difference.

---

**Section.** What matters first (hierarchy): applies.

**Findings**
1. **Where headings are clearly larger than the text, do they also differ from it in weight, form, or color?** The title "Book a workshop seat" (x 96–397, y 60–95) and the four field labels ("Workshop name" y ≈ 134, "Preferred date" y ≈ 240, "Number of seats" y ≈ 346, "Notes for the host" y ≈ 452) use the same bold weight and the same near-black colour. Size alone separates them. Because the size step is large (about 1.75×), the viewer still finds the title first. But every line on the page is equally heavy, so the page reads as one flat level with a bigger first line, and nothing quieter sits beneath the labels. Fix: keep the title bold and set the labels lighter, in a medium or regular weight or a slightly softer grey. That gives the title contrast from weight as well as size, and the labels' weight is left free to mark something like a required field. Convention (typography canon: contrast from more than size; *Refactoring UI*: use weight and colour, not only size). Weight: minor. I could not open the reference entry in this session, so the convention wording is mine, not the entry's.

**What's working.**
- **A clear starting point:** the title is the only large element on an otherwise quiet page, so the eye knows where to begin and what the page is for in one glance.
- **A tight two-level scale:** there is one title size and one label size, with no near-duplicate sizes. Nothing looks like a mistake and every size has an obvious job.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 2 yes, 1 no (headings differ from text by more than size)

sections.report:
**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies. (I couldn't run the crop script because Bash was refused, so I worked from the whole image, which is about 1280×800 and one screen tall. Pixel positions are by eye.)

**Findings**
1. **Does the arrangement lead the eye from the first element through the rest, with no line, gaze, or pointing shape that leads it off the edge?** No. The eye goes from the heading (x≈96, y≈60–92) down the four label-and-field pairs and stops at the "Notes for the host" field (bottom at y≈513). After that there is nothing: no "Book" or submit button and no summary, only about 280 px of blank page down to the bottom edge. The empty band is inside the frame, so this isn't a cut-off capture. A viewer who fills in the last field has nowhere to go. They are left looking for how to finish the booking, and some will think the page didn't load. An eye path needs an end point, usually the call to action, so the viewer never hits a dead end (Arnheim, *The Power of the Center*, under "Clear eye path"). Fix: end the column with the action. Put a primary "Book seat(s)" button on the same left edge (x=96) at the same ~37 px gap as the fields, so the form's own rhythm carries the eye onto it. This overlaps the Interface section, which will probably file the missing button too. Here the point is that the layout has no end point. **Defect. Major.**
2. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No. Every element sits in a 480 px column at x≈96–576, which is less than half the width. The right ~700 px and the bottom third are empty, and nothing on the right balances the column. The page looks like a left-hand panel whose other half never loaded, and the blank area reads as left over, not chosen. A heavy side needs a counterweight (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance"). Fix, either of two ways: (a) give the right side a job, such as workshop details, the date, price or seats left. A booking page needs those anyway, and they would balance the column. Or (b) make the emptiness clearly deliberate by setting the form in a centred or bounded container with a visible edge, so the open space frames the form instead of trailing off. A left-aligned form column is a normal web convention, so this costs less than finding 1: it hurts how finished the page looks, not whether it can be filled in. **Taste/convention. Minor.**

**What's working.**
- One strong left edge. The heading, labels and fields all start exactly at x=96, with no near-misses, so the column reads as one ordered stack. Keep that edge for anything you add, including the button.
- The spacing shows the pairs. Each label sits about 10 px above its own field, and the next label is about 37 px below the field before it. Each label clearly belongs to the field under it, and the rhythm down the column is even and easy to follow.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (visual weight balances; arrangement leads the eye through to an end point)

It reads as a plain, neutral booking form. **Job (assumed):** a web form where a visitor books seats at a workshop.

**Walk, Color (9 lines):**
- Small palette: yes. Only near-black text (about #1F2328), blue-gray field borders and a white background, with no hue at all.
- Saturated color kept to a small share: yes. There is no saturated color.

- Warm forward, cool back: yes. Nothing is warm. The borders are a slightly cool gray. No element needs to come forward through temperature here. The missing submit action belongs to the interface and whole-piece sections.
- Matching colors look the same: yes. All four borders and all labels match.
- No vibrating edges: yes.
- Status colors used for their usual meaning: yes. There are none.
- Meaning not shown by color alone: yes. Color carries no meaning.
- Dark theme not pure black: yes. It's a light theme, so this doesn't apply.

No line came out `no` or `unsure`, so there were no entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** The fully neutral palette suits a plain utility form. Near-black labels on white and blue-gray field borders (around x 96–576, y 152–514) give three clear steps of lightness. The labels, the inputs and the empty page stay distinct without any hue, and there's no accent competing for attention. This leaves room for one action color when a submit button is added. The field borders also look dark enough to see as edges against white, which matters for inputs. The exact border contrast against the 3:1 component rule (WCAG 1.4.11) should be measured.

sections.report:
**Walk (working notes)**

First read: the eye lands on "Book a workshop seat", then goes down four bordered fields of the same size. The form has no button and nothing below the last field, so the eye stops at "Notes for the host" with nowhere to go. It reads as a plain web booking form for a member of the public. Image is about one screen (1280×800), so I worked from the whole image; the crop and entries scripts can't run because Bash was refused.

Interface:
- One primary action: **no**, there is no submit button anywhere.
- Controls look like what they do: yes (bordered boxes read as fields).
- Borders reach 3:1: **unsure**. The mid-grey border (~#8892a0) on white looks like about 3:1, so it's borderline.
- Hover/pressed/disabled shown: yes, none are shown.
- Focus indicator: unsure, can't see it in a still.
- Focus not obscured: yes. Content not covered: yes.
- Target size: yes. Fields look about 480×44 px.
- Phone thumb zone: yes, this is not a phone layout.
- Status/where am I: yes for a single-step form.
- Way out: **no**, there's no cancel or back.
- Valid values only: **no**. Date, seats, and workshop name are all plain text boxes, with no date picker, stepper, or select.
- Destructive set apart: yes, there are none.
- Recognition over recall: **no**. "Workshop name" is free text, so the user has to remember and type the exact name.
- Progressive disclosure: yes.
- Labels: yes, each sits above its own field and is closer to it.
- Natural mapping: yes. Single column: yes.
- Required/optional marked: **no**. Nothing is marked, and the notes field is presumably optional.
- Errors in words / error says fix: yes, no errors are shown.
- Empty state: yes, none.
- Help near step: yes for a simple task.
- Shortcuts: yes, not needed here.
- Anticipation: **no**. No prefilled workshop (the user likely arrived from one), no default of 1 seat, and no next action.
- Platform conventions: **no**. A single-line box is used for free-form notes where a multi-line textarea is the convention, and there's no submit button at the end of the form.
- Audience's words: yes. Link purpose: yes. Sensory instructions: yes. Conceptual model: yes. Consistency across screens: yes. Reflow: yes. Honest choices: yes.

The deep read of the entries was not possible (Bash refused). The `no` answers stand on what can be seen. The border contrast stays a borderline `no`, to be confirmed with a measurement.

---

**Section.** Interface: applies (a four-field booking form).

**Findings**
1. **Is exactly one button styled as the primary action, with every other action styled lower?** There is no button anywhere. The form ends at the "Notes for the host" field (y≈470–514) and is followed by about 280 px of empty white. A user who fills in all four fields has no way to book the seat and no sign of what happens next. The form can't do its job. If the button exists but didn't render, the capture is wrong; otherwise this is a missing core control. Fix: add one clearly primary button (e.g. "Book seat") directly under the last field, left-aligned with the fields. Defect. Weight: major.
2. **Do the inputs allow only valid values, by pickers, input types, or disabled options?** "Preferred date" (y≈258–302) and "Number of seats" (y≈364–408) look identical to the free-text name field. Nothing shows a date picker, a calendar icon, a number stepper, or a format hint. Users will type dates in any format and could enter "two" or 0 for seats, which leads to errors or wrong bookings. Fix: give the date field a date picker (ideally limited to the workshop's real dates) and the seats field a number stepper with min 1 and the max available. Defect (Nielsen 5, error prevention; Norman, constraints). Weight: major.
3. **Is everything the user needs to act visible on this screen, with nothing to remember from another?** "Workshop name" (y≈152–196) is an empty free-text field. The user has to recall and spell the workshop's exact name, and a typo means a booking the host can't match. Fix: make it a select or searchable list of open workshops, or prefill it from the workshop page the user came from. Defect (Nielsen 6). Weight: major.
4. **Does the screen put what the user likely needs next in front of them?** Every field starts empty: no prefilled workshop, no default of 1 seat, and no next action (see 1). The user does all the work for what is usually a one-click intent. Fix: prefill the workshop and its date from context and default seats to 1. Taste/convention (Tognazzini's anticipation; the source is off the approved list, so this is common sense here). Weight: minor (much of it is covered by 2 and 3).
5. **Do the navigation and components follow the conventions users know?** "Notes for the host" (y≈470–514) is a one-line box the same height as the others. Users expect a multi-line textarea for free notes, and a single line suggests only a few words are welcome. Fix: use a textarea about 3–4 lines tall. Convention (Jakob's law). Weight: minor.
6. **Are required or optional fields marked?** None of the four labels says required or optional. "Notes for the host" is almost certainly optional, and the user can't tell, so they may stall or meet surprise errors. Fix: mark the one optional field "(optional)", or mark required fields consistently. Convention. Weight: minor.
7. **Does every dialog, flow, or state shown have a visible way out?** There's no cancel or back link, and nothing on the page links back to the workshop list. That costs little on a standalone page with browser Back available, but it matters if this is a modal or embedded step. Fix: add a quiet "Cancel" or "Back to workshops" link, styled lower than the primary button. Convention (Nielsen 3). Weight: minor.
8. **Do input borders reach 3:1 contrast?** The mid-grey field borders (all four fields, x≈96–576) look borderline, around 3:1 against white. If they fall short, low-vision users lose the field edges. Fix: measure the border colour; if it's under 3:1, darken it a step. Convention (WCAG 1.4.11). Weight: minor.

**What's working.** Each label is bold, sits directly above its own field, and is clearly closer to that field than to the one above (about 8 px label-to-field vs about 40 px between groups), so there is no doubt which label goes with which box. The single column with full-width fields of equal size gives a clean top-to-bottom path with no zig-zag.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The focus indicator on the fields (a mid-grey border alone wouldn't be enough). How the form shows validation errors and success after submitting, which matters a lot here given the free-text date and seats fields.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 24 yes, 8 no (one primary action; visible way out; inputs allow only valid values; recognition rather than recall; required/optional marked; anticipation; platform conventions; input border contrast), 1 unsure (focus indicator)
